citation: Thomas Forsyth, "An account of the Manners and Customs of the Sauk and Fox Nations of Indians Tradition", printed in Emma Helen Blair (ed.), The Indian Tribes of the Upper Mississippi Valley and Region of the Great Lakes, vol. II (Cleveland: The Arthur H. Clark Company, 1912), pp. 183-245, with notes by Blair and by William R. Gerard.
author: Thomas Forsyth, United States agent to the Sauk and Fox at Fort Armstrong (Rock River agency); Emma Helen Blair, editor; William R. Gerard (note 87 on the cat-tail flag)
date: 1912 (this printing); Forsyth's manuscript, in the Draper Collection's Forsyth Papers, was written about 1827 (it reports a conversation of 'summer (1826)')
describes_date: The Sauk and Fox of the 1810s-1820s, from an agent's years among them
repository: Internet Archive, item indiantribesofup02blaiiala (University of California Libraries copy).
locator: Vol. II pp. 227-28 (the bark summer houses, 'built in the form of an oblong ... a door at each end'; the winter lodges of poles 'in two rows ... covering them with mats made of what they call puc-wy', the bearskin door, the smoke out the top; 'spits to roast their meat on'), note 87 on p. 227 (Gerard: puc-wy is the cat-tail flag, Typha latifolia, 'used for making mats for covering wigwams'), p. 233 (families 'who have a sufficiency of horses to transport their families and baggage', and those with none going by canoe). Read in the Internet Archive's OCR text, located by the printed running heads.
access_notes: Fetched 2026-11-03 from archive.org as the djvu text (T-3342); the quotations were checked against that text. Not read off the page images.
note: An agent's description of the Sauk and Fox, the Potawatomi's western neighbours and close kin in language and way of life, in the years around 1812. It does not describe Chicago or the Potawatomi. T-3342 reads it for what a camp of these lake and prairie peoples was made of: mat lodges on bent poles, bark summer houses, roasting spits, horses and canoes for carrying families and baggage.
what_it_supplies: the mat lodge's frame and covering: poles driven in two rows and bent over, covered with cat-tail mats, a skin hung for the door, the fire in the middle and the smoke out the top (pp. 227-28)
the bark summer house: an oblong with a door at each end and a bench down each long side (p. 227)
the roasting spit as a mark of a camp (p. 228)
horses and canoes as the two ways a family and its baggage travelled (p. 233)
what_it_does_not_supply: anything about Chicago, the Potawatomi or August 1812
a size for any lodge, except that some bark houses were 'fifty or sixty feet long'
a picture of any of it
